summary: The visual-quality gap is primarily upstream of SPEAR: restaurant_kitchen_1000sqft was created by a local bpy primitive/blockout script, not by Infinigen-Indoors scene generation. SPEAR imported and cooked what it was given. Infinigen-Indoors can produce photorealistic residential-style indoor kitchens, but the local and official asset/semantic coverage does not appear to include a genuine restaurant/commercial kitchen directly. Best path for a photoreal SPEAR-live-ready commercial kitchen is hybrid: use Infinigen for room/layout/material inspiration where useful, then replace blockout geometry with high-quality commercial kitchen assets and Unreal-native materials/lights.

findings.message: restaurant_kitchen_1000sqft is not an Infinigen-Indoors generated kitchen. runner.sh activates the infinigen env, but calls .control-tower/runs/.../scripts/create_restaurant_kitchen_1000sqft.py directly. That script constructs the scene from bpy primitive cubes/cylinders with simple Principled materials. Source scene stats confirm blockout scale: 235 mesh objects, 2,848 vertices, 1,894 polygons, 17 materials, 1 image, 2.5 MB blend. This is the main reason it appears like random primitive shapes.

The export/import path preserved the primitive scene rather than causing the blockout. SPEAR imported 235 static mesh assets and spawned 235 actors with expected bounds, and validation/pak verification succeeded. The import log shows materials/textures enabled, but source materials are flat colors; exported textures were 820 PNGs all at 256x256 totaling only 3.4 MB, and the FBX was 3.9 MB.

Unreal import produced 235 'No smoothing group information' warnings, one per static mesh. This can worsen faceted primitive appearance, especially cylinders and bevels, but it is secondary to the low-detail source geometry and flat material authoring.

The current export used -r 256, below Infinigen's documented example of -r 1024 for baked texture maps. Official export docs state the process is lossy and only handles Albedo, Roughness, Normal, and Metallicity maps; other procedural material features are ignored. Source: https://github.com/princeton-vl/infinigen/blob/main/docs/ExportingToExternalFileFormats.md

Official Infinigen-Indoors does target photorealistic indoor scenes with furniture, architecture elements, appliances, day-to-day objects, and a constraint solver. It also documents a Kitchen room generation command. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11824 and https://github.com/princeton-vl/infinigen/blob/main/docs/HelloRoom.md

Local Infinigen coverage appears residential, not commercial restaurant. Local tags/semantics include Kitchen, BreakRoom, MeetingRoom, etc., but no Restaurant or CommercialKitchen. KitchenAppliance maps to DishwasherFactory, OvenFactory, BeverageFridgeFactory, and MicrowaveFactory; commercial fixtures such as ranges, fryers, exhaust hoods, prep tables, walk-in coolers, NSF shelving, and dish stations are absent from the standard semantics inspected.

A true local Infinigen indoor scene is materially and geometrically different from the current restaurant result: /outputs/indoors_gpu/coarse/scene.blend has 172 mesh objects, 174 materials, 148 images, about 2.4M vertices, and 3.0M polygons. This supports the conclusion that the restaurant result did not exercise Infinigen-Indoors quality.

For whole-scene simulator export, official docs emphasize USDC/Omniverse workflows; whole indoor scenes are documented/tested for IsaacSim, while SPEAR's current setup path imports FBX via Unreal. FBX can work for small/simple scenes but should be treated as a lossy bridge, especially for materials and complex procedural detail. Source: https://github.com/princeton-vl/infinigen/blob/main/docs/ExportingToSimulators.md

Infinigen supports adding external static assets, including .glb/.gltf/.fbx/.blend, and recommends correct size/orientation/semantics for placement. This is the best official hook for a commercial-kitchen hybrid workflow. Source: https://github.com/princeton-vl/infinigen/blob/main/docs/StaticAssets.md

follow_up_recommendations: Rank 1, highest fidelity: build the commercial kitchen as an Unreal/SPEAR-native kitbash using licensed photoreal commercial kitchen assets, PBR stainless/ceramic/rubber materials, Lumen/rect fixture lighting, collision, and player-start validation. Use the current primitive scene only as a rough spatial brief, not as final geometry.

Rank 2, best Infinigen-first hybrid: generate a real Infinigen-Indoors Kitchen or custom floor plan for shell/layout, then replace commercial equipment placeholders with external GLB/FBX assets via Infinigen static_assets or a post-generation Blender placement pass. Export with at least r1024/r2048 for baked maps where using Infinigen materials, but import major kitbash assets directly into Unreal to preserve material quality.

Rank 3, fastest Infinigen validation: run an official residential Kitchen scene with infinigen_examples.generate_indoors, remove fast_solve.gin for quality, use real_geometry.gin or real_geometry_with_bump.gin where compatible, and export/import a small r1024 FBX/USDC test. This will validate the SPEAR bridge on real Infinigen output, but it will not satisfy the commercial restaurant requirement by itself.

Rank 4, low-effort rescue of current run: shade smooth/apply normals, add smoothing-group-compatible export, increase bake resolution to r1024, replace flat color materials with procedural/PBR textures, add decals/dirt/edge wear, and add more mesh detail. This can improve readability but will remain a blockout and is not recommended as the photoreal target.

Before the next Builder/Experimenter packet, require validation checks: Blender source has materially higher geometric complexity than the current 2,848-vertex scene; exported textures are at intended resolution; Unreal import has no systemic smoothing/material warnings; a screenshot/live run verifies scale, spawn, collision, exposure, fixture lighting, flashlight response, and recognizable commercial-kitchen silhouettes.

If Tower chooses the hybrid path, define an asset manifest first: cooking line, ventilation hood, prep tables, shelving, dishwashing, sinks, walk-in/reach-in refrigeration, floor/wall/ceiling surfaces, small props, and fixture lights. Validate licenses before adding assets to the repo/pak.
memory_worthy: restaurant_kitchen_1000sqft visual gap diagnosis: generated by a custom bpy cube/cylinder script, not real Infinigen-Indoors; source scene has 235 meshes but only 2,848 vertices/1,894 polygons and flat simple materials. SPEAR import/cook succeeded, so quality issue is upstream source content plus low r256 bake/smoothing warnings.

Infinigen-Indoors can generate photorealistic residential indoor kitchens, but local inspected semantics/assets do not include restaurant/commercial kitchen support; recommended path is Infinigen layout or shell plus external photoreal commercial kitchen assets imported/assembled for Unreal/SPEAR.
